text: PCT (Patent Cooperation Treaty) Filing: The PCT allows inventors to file a single international patent application that has effect in over 150 member countries. For Indian applicants, the PCT national phase entry deadline is 31 months from the priority date. The Indian Patent Office is a Receiving Office (RO) and International Searching Authority (ISA). PCT filing fees for Indian natural persons start at approximately INR 10,000 for international filing fee plus INR 7,000 for search fee. PCT provides 18 extra months compared to direct national filings.

Convention Priority under Paris Convention: Under Article 4 of the Paris Convention, an applicant who files a patent application in one member country has 12 months to file corresponding applications in other member countries while claiming priority from the first filing date. This is called 'convention priority'. For AYUSH innovations, claiming Indian priority is strategic as it establishes the earliest possible date, protecting against any subsequent disclosures. The priority document must be submitted within 3 months of filing in India.

Direct National Phase Entry in India: Foreign applicants can enter the Indian national phase from a PCT application within 31 months from the priority date. Required documents include: (1) Complete specification in English, (2) Claims, (3) Abstract, (4) Drawings if any, (5) Priority document, (6) Assignment deed if different from PCT applicant, (7) Power of Attorney. The Indian Patent Office requires fee payment at national phase entry — INR 8,000 for natural persons, INR 40,000 for others (e-filing rates).

WIPO Traditional Knowledge Resources: WIPO's Intergovernmental Committee on Intellectual Property and Genetic Resources, Traditional Knowledge and Folklore (IGC) is developing international legal instruments for TK protection. India actively participates in these negotiations. WIPO also maintains databases and provides technical assistance for documenting traditional knowledge. AYUSH innovators should be aware of ongoing international developments that may affect TK-based patents.

TRIPS Agreement and Traditional Knowledge: The TRIPS Agreement (Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) sets minimum IP standards for WTO members. Article 27.3(b) allows countries to exclude plants and animals from patentability. India uses this flexibility through Section 3(p) of the Patents Act to exclude traditional knowledge from patentability. However, TRIPS does not mandate TK disclosure requirements — India has proposed amendments requiring patent applicants to disclose the source of biological materials and TK used.

Nagoya Protocol on ABS: The Nagoya Protocol (2010) under the Convention on Biological Diversity establishes an international framework for Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS). Key provisions include: (1) Prior Informed Consent (PIC) from provider countries, (2) Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT) for benefit sharing, (3) Compliance checkpoints in user countries. India ratified the Nagoya Protocol in 2012. The NBA and SBBs implement these provisions domestically through the Biological Diversity Act 2002.

Madrid Protocol for Trademarks: While patents protect inventions, AYUSH product names and formulation brands can be protected through trademarks. The Madrid Protocol allows international trademark registration through a single application. India joined the Madrid Protocol in 2013. AYUSH manufacturers exporting products should consider trademark registration in target markets. Geographical Indications (GI) provide additional protection for region-specific AYUSH products like Darjeeling Tea or Kashmir Saffron.
